dataset.what_one_row_represents: One CMS Timely-and-Effective-Care measure for one US state or territory in the 2023-Q1 to 2024-Q1 reporting window.
dataset.geographic_scope: All 50 US states + DC + 5 US territories (PR, GU, AS, MP, VI)

ana_01.label: 1,232 rows = 56 jurisdictions x 22 measures
ana_01.content: The dataset is a tidy long table: 1,232 rows, 8 columns. Each row is one (state, measure) pair. There are 56 jurisdictions (50 states, DC, and the territories PR, GU, AS, MP, VI), 22 unique measure_ids covering 21 distinct measure_names (CMS uses two IDs for one of the OP_18b/OP_18c psychiatric variants), and 6 conditions: Emergency Department, Sepsis Care, Healthcare Personnel Vaccination, Cataract surgery outcome, Colonoscopy care, and Electronic Clinical Quality Measure. Reporting periods range from 2023-01-01 to 2024-03-31.

calculation.output:
rows: 1232
cols: 8
unique states/territories: 56
unique measure_ids: 22
unique measure_names: 21
unique conditions: 6
date range: 2023-01-01 -> 2024-03-31

data_table.description: Dataset shape summary

ana_02.label: 12.6% of scores are missing — concentrated in territories
ana_02.content: 155 of 1,232 score cells (12.6%) are blank. Missingness is concentrated in two ways. By measure, OP_31 (cataract vision improvement) has 78.6% missing — only 12 jurisdictions report it; the four OP_18b/c high-acuity sub-measures each miss 14.3%. By state, the four small territories drive the bulk: Northern Mariana Islands, American Samoa, US Virgin Islands, and Guam each have 22 missing values, meaning they report essentially nothing (footnote 5). Among the 50 states + DC + PR, missingness drops to a few rows per state, mostly in the lowest-volume sub-acuity slices for small-population states.

calculation.output:
missing scores: 155 of 1232 (12.6%)
OP_31: 78.6%
OP_18*_HIGH/LOW/VERY_HIGH: 14.3% each
MP/AS/VI/GU: 22 missing rows each

data_table.description: States with most missing rows (top 8)

ana_03.label: Six conditions, ED dominates with 12 measures
ana_03.content: The 22 measure_ids partition into 6 conditions. Emergency Department is by far the largest at 12 measures (the OP_18b/c family, OP_22, OP_23) and 672 rows. Sepsis Care has 5 measures (280 rows). Healthcare Personnel Vaccination has 2 (HCP_COVID_19 and IMM_3, 112 rows). Cataract, Colonoscopy, and the opioid Electronic Clinical Quality Measure each have a single measure (56 rows each). This means roughly 55% of the dataset's content is about emergency-department flow.

calculation.output:
Emergency Department: 12 measures, 672 rows
Sepsis Care: 5 measures, 280 rows
Healthcare Personnel Vaccination: 2, 112
Cataract / Colonoscopy / ECQM: 1 measure each, 56 rows

data_table.description: Measure count and row count by condition

ana_04.label: OP_18b: 110 to 310 minutes, a 2.82x national spread
ana_04.content: Across 52 reporting jurisdictions, the median ED visit (OP_18b) ranges from 110 minutes in North Dakota to 310 minutes in Washington DC — a 2.82x ratio. The mean across jurisdictions is 161 minutes (within rounding of the CMS-reported 161-minute national median for 2024) with a standard deviation of 42 minutes. Fifty percent of jurisdictions sit between 133 and 174 minutes — a 41-minute interquartile band. The cross-jurisdiction median is 154 minutes, indicating a right skew driven by a handful of jurisdictions with very long waits.

data_table.description: OP_18b summary statistics across 52 reporting jurisdictions

ana_05.label: Top 10 longest ED waits — DC and PR tower over the rest
ana_05.content: The longest median ED times all sit on the Eastern seaboard or in the territories. DC leads at 310 minutes, with Puerto Rico close behind at 302. After a 50-minute gap, Maryland (251), Rhode Island (224), and Delaware (217) form a second tier. Massachusetts (216), New York (199), Connecticut (193), North Carolina (192), and New Jersey (187) round out the top 10. Nine of the top 10 are in the Northeast / Mid-Atlantic corridor — the densest, most insurance-volatile, and most boarding-affected region of the country.

data_table.description: Top 10 longest median ED times (minutes)

ana_06.label: Top 10 shortest ED waits — Plains and rural West
ana_06.content: The shortest waits cluster in the Great Plains and rural West. North Dakota leads at 110 minutes, followed by South Dakota (113), Nebraska (114), Hawaii (115), Oklahoma (119), Iowa and Kansas (both 120), Minnesota and Indiana (both 125), and Mississippi (127). The fastest jurisdiction (ND) is under two hours; the slowest (DC) is over five. Hawaii is the lone non-Plains-or-Mountain entrant — a useful reminder that the geography is about hospital capacity per capita, not climate.

data_table.description: Top 10 shortest median ED times (minutes)

ana_07.label: Full 52-state OP_18b table for choropleth and dot strip
ana_07.content: The complete state-by-state median ED time table, in ascending order, runs from ND at 1.83 hours to DC at 5.17 hours. This is the canonical chart-ready table that drives both the choropleth map and the ranked dot-strip in the blog.

calculation.output: Full 52-row state/score/hours table emitted for charts.

data_table.description: OP_18b for all reporting jurisdictions, with hours and territory flag

ana_08.label: Acuity gradient: high-volume EDs add ~66 min over low-volume
ana_08.content: OP_18b is reported by ED volume tier (Low / Medium / High / Very High). National medians climb monotonically: Low-volume EDs report 126 minutes, Medium 168, High 184, Very High 192 — a 66-minute jump from the smallest to the busiest sites. State-level gaps inside this same data are often dramatic: New Mexico's Very-High-volume EDs run 164 minutes longer than its Low-volume EDs (134 -> 298 min). Indiana is the outlier in the other direction (-5 min — its busiest EDs are slightly faster than its smallest). The size of the within-state acuity gap is itself a hospital-system-design signal, separate from a state's headline OP_18b.

calculation.output: national medians: Low 126, Medium 168, High 184, Very High 192 min. NM range 164 min; IN range -5 min.

data_table.description: National median ED time by hospital volume tier

ana_09.label: OP_22 LWBS: DC's 6% leaves the ED before being seen
ana_09.content: OP_22 measures the share of patients who left the ED before being seen — a direct symptom of overcrowding. The cross-state mean is 2.5% and the median 2.0%. DC is again the extreme at 6%, with Massachusetts, Delaware, and Rhode Island tied at 5%. Mississippi, Maryland, Missouri, Oregon, and Illinois sit at 4%. The 'best' tier — Utah, Idaho, Puerto Rico, Nebraska, Wyoming — reports 1%. PR is unusual here: it has the second-longest ED time in the country yet the lowest LWBS rate, suggesting patients there wait but do not leave.

calculation.output: n=52, mean 2.54%, median 2.00%, max 6.0%; DC 6, MA/DE/RI 5; UT/ID/PR/NE/WY 1

data_table.description: OP_22 LWBS percentage by state (full table, sorted desc)

ana_10.label: OP_23 stroke imaging: huge state spread, DC at 26%
ana_10.content: OP_23 measures the share of stroke patients who get a head CT or MRI within 45 minutes of ED arrival — the most time-critical workflow in emergency medicine. The cross-state mean is 67% and median 69%, but the spread is enormous: DC reports just 26%, New Mexico 41%, Vermont 44%, while South Carolina and Wisconsin lead at 78%. A 52-percentage-point gap between the worst- and best-performing jurisdictions for a measure with a hard 45-minute deadline is the single largest disparity for a higher-better measure in the file.

calculation.output: n=52, mean 66.5%, median 69.0%; top SC/WI 78, MO/IN 77, NJ 74; bottom DC 26, NM 41, VT 44, SD 54, WY 56

data_table.description: OP_23 stroke imaging within 45 min — top and bottom 5

ana_11.label: Long ED + high LWBS travel together (r=0.48)
ana_11.content: The Pearson correlation between OP_18b and OP_22 across 52 jurisdictions is r = 0.48, moderate-strong. The eight jurisdictions that score worst on the combined z-score (long waits AND high walkout rate) are DC, RI, DE, MA, MD, PR, IL, NY — a roster that overlaps almost completely with the longest-ED-time top 10. Puerto Rico is the one telling exception: it has the second-worst ED time but a low walkout rate, dragging its combined score below DC's by a full 4.4 z-units.

calculation.output: Pearson r = 0.482 (n=52). Top combined z: DC 6.44, RI 3.57, DE 3.40, MA 3.38, MD 3.36, PR 2.01, IL 1.52, NY 1.28

data_table.description: Top 8 jurisdictions by combined z-score (OP_18b z + OP_22 z)

ana_12.label: HCP COVID up-to-date: median 11%, mean 15%, max 62%
ana_12.content: Healthcare-personnel COVID-19 'up-to-date' coverage (HCP_COVID_19) is the lowest-coverage measure in the entire dataset. Across 52 reporting jurisdictions the mean is 15.2%, the median is just 11.1%, and 20 jurisdictions report 10% or less — including 4 that are at or below 5%. The only outlier on the high end is Puerto Rico at 62%, which is more than triple the mainland median.

calculation.output: mean 15.2, median 11.1, min 2.7, max 62.0; n_le_10 = 20; n_le_5 = 4

data_table.description: HCP_COVID_19 distribution summary

ana_13.label: HCW COVID ranking: PR 62% leads, AR 2.7% trails
ana_13.content: The state-level ranking spans 23x — Puerto Rico's 62.0% to Arkansas's 2.7%. The top 10 states (PR, MA, DE, VT, IL, NJ, OR, LA, OH, NH) include several Northeast/Midwest states with strong workplace mandate histories. The bottom 10 (MO, VA, AK, DC, FL, AL, ND, ID, SD, AR) span the rural Plains and parts of the South. Notably, DC has the lowest ED times' opposite extreme — among the worst HCW COVID coverage rates at 6.6% — even though DC also has the longest ED waits.

data_table.description: Top and bottom 10 states by HCP_COVID_19 up-to-date %

ana_14.label: Full 52-state HCP_COVID_19 table
ana_14.content: The full ranked HCW COVID up-to-date list across all 52 reporting jurisdictions is available for the choropleth and the side-by-side comparison with flu coverage. PR is a clean outlier; below it the distribution is roughly long-tailed with most mainland states clustered between 5% and 25%.

calculation.output: All 52 states printed in descending order by COVID pct

data_table.description: HCP_COVID_19 up-to-date %, all 52 jurisdictions

ana_15.label: Flu vaccination among HCW: median 82.5%, range 58-96
ana_15.content: By contrast with COVID, healthcare-personnel influenza coverage (IMM_3) is high. Across 52 jurisdictions, the mean is 80.8%, the median 82.5%, the minimum 58 (Montana) and maximum 96 (Maine). The interquartile range is a relatively tight 74.8 to 88.0 — every state vaccinates the great majority of its hospital workforce against flu.

data_table.description: IMM_3 flu vaccination among HCW — distribution summary

ana_16.label: Same workforce, same workplaces — 65.6 pp flu/COVID gap
ana_16.content: Inside the very same hospitals, the same employees who get flu shots overwhelmingly do not stay current on COVID boosters. The mean state-level gap (flu pct - COVID pct) is 65.6 percentage points. The smallest gap is Puerto Rico at -3 pp (covid actually higher than flu — a complete inversion). The widest gap is DC at 87.4 pp (94% flu, 6.6% COVID). Twelve states have gaps above 80 pp. This is a within-hospital signal: the same processes that achieve >80% flu coverage are not being applied to COVID, indicating a policy and motivation gap rather than an access gap.

calculation.output: national medians: covid 11.1%, flu 82.5%; mean gap 65.6 pp; smallest PR -3.0 pp; largest DC 87.4 pp

data_table.description: Flu - COVID gap (percentage points) for all 52 jurisdictions

ana_17.label: Higher COVID coverage tracks longer ED times (r=0.44)
ana_17.content: Counterintuitively, jurisdictions with higher HCP_COVID_19 coverage tend to have longer ED times. Pearson r = 0.44 (Spearman 0.25) across the 52 jurisdictions. This does NOT imply boosters slow down EDs — both are downstream of population density, hospital occupancy, and policy environment: the urban, blue-state, mandate-friendly jurisdictions (MA, NJ, IL) sit toward the top on both axes, while rural Plains states (ND, SD, NE) sit toward the bottom on both. PR is the standout outlier: 62% covid + 302-min ED, far above the trend line in both directions.

calculation.output: Pearson r = 0.441 (n=52); Spearman rho = 0.248

data_table.description: Scatter data: HCP_COVID_19 % vs OP_18b minutes for all 52

ana_18.label: SEP_1 sepsis bundle: median 60.5%, PR floor at 16%
ana_18.content: Compliance with the SEP_1 severe-sepsis-and-septic-shock bundle has a national median of 60.5% — almost exactly matching the high-50s benchmark in the literature. Across 52 jurisdictions the mean is 60.6%, std 8.5, with the IQR running 58 to 65. Top performers: Colorado 73%, Maine 72%, Montana, Utah, Hawaii all 71%. Bottom: North Dakota 54%, DC 49%, New Mexico 48%, Delaware 48%, and Puerto Rico an extreme outlier at 16%.

calculation.output: n=52, mean 60.6, std 8.5, median 60.5, min 16; top CO 73, ME 72, MT/UT/HI 71; bottom ND 54, DC 49, NM 48, DE 48, PR 16

data_table.description: SEP_1 — top 5 and bottom 5 states

ana_19.label: All 12 process measures side by side — sepsis ceiling, stroke ceiling, COVID floor
ana_19.content: Looking at the 12 process measures together reveals the topology of US hospital quality. The 'engineered floor' bundles — severe sepsis 6-hour (median 91%), septic shock 6-hour (84%), colonoscopy follow-up rec (93%) — show that when CMS standardizes a process, compliance approaches the ceiling. The 'engineered floor' measures (LWBS at 2%, SEP_1 at 60.5%, opioid co-prescribing at 15%) represent open problems where wide variation persists. HCW COVID coverage at a national median of 11% sits in a category of its own: half the values in this entire dataset are above 80%, but COVID is at the floor.

calculation.output: 12-measure summary table: n, min, median, mean, max printed for each of SEP_1, SEV_SEP_3HR, SEV_SEP_6HR, SEP_SH_3HR, SEP_SH_6HR, OP_22, OP_23, OP_29, OP_31, SAFE_USE_OF_OPIOIDS, IMM_3, HCP_COVID_19

data_table.description: Cross-state distribution of every process measure (n, min, median, max, direction)

ana_20.label: Sepsis compliance and HCW COVID coverage move in opposite directions
ana_20.content: Pearson r between SEP_1 compliance and HCP_COVID_19 coverage across states is -0.56 — a moderate negative correlation. States that get sepsis bundles right (CO, MT, UT) report low HCW COVID coverage, while states with high HCW COVID (PR, DE) sit at or near the SEP_1 floor. This contradicts a simple 'good hospitals do everything well' story and is the strongest signal in the dataset that 'quality' is not a single dimension — different process measures answer to different organizational forces.

calculation.output: Pearson r = -0.558 (n=52)

data_table.description: Pearson r summary

ana_21.label: Concurrent opioid+benzo prescribing: NH 19% highest
ana_21.content: SAFE_USE_OF_OPIOIDS measures concurrent prescribing of opioids and benzodiazepines (lower is better). The cross-state mean is 14.4% with a median of 15%. The highest (worst) rates are in New England — New Hampshire 19%, Massachusetts 18%, Connecticut 18% — alongside Nebraska 18% and New Jersey 17%. The lowest rates: Puerto Rico 3%, Mississippi 11%, Arizona 11%, DC 11%, Hawaii 11%. The five-fold range tells a clear regional-prescribing story: New England prescribes the most, the South-Atlantic and Pacific the least.

calculation.output: n=52, mean 14.44, median 15.00; bottom (best) PR 3, MS/AZ/DC/HI 11; top (worst) NH 19, MA/CT/NE 18, NJ 17

data_table.description: Top 5 worst and best states for SAFE_USE_OF_OPIOIDS

ana_22.label: Five logical measure groups
ana_22.content: Reorganized by what they measure rather than CMS condition labels, the 22 measure_ids form 5 buckets: ED flow (12 measures — OP_18b/c family + OP_22 + OP_23), Vaccination (2 — HCP_COVID_19, IMM_3), Sepsis (5 — SEP_1, SEV_SEP_3HR, SEV_SEP_6HR, SEP_SH_3HR, SEP_SH_6HR), Outpatient procedures (2 — OP_29 colonoscopy, OP_31 cataract), and Pharmacy safety (1 — SAFE_USE_OF_OPIOIDS). This taxonomy is more useful for narrative than the CMS 6-condition split because it groups measures by what an analyst can do with them.

calculation.output: ED flow: 12; Vaccination: 2; Sepsis: 5; Outpatient procedures: 2; Pharmacy safety: 1; TOTAL 22

data_table.description: Five logical measure groups

caveats.content: OP_18b and similar averages include VHA and DoD hospital data per footnotes 25 and 26. State-level numbers therefore reflect federal hospitals operating in those states, not solely civilian hospitals.

Four US territories (MP, AS, VI, GU) report essentially nothing (22 missing rows each, footnote 5). They are excluded from all numeric analyses but kept visible in tables to acknowledge the geographic scope.
OP_31 (cataract surgery vision improvement) is reported by only 12 jurisdictions; any cross-state inference from it is fragile.
Reporting periods differ across measures (some cover a full year, some a single quarter). Comparisons across measures within a state should not be read as same-period snapshots.
Correlations across states are state-level (n=52). A state-level association between, for example, HCW COVID coverage and ED time does not establish a hospital-level or patient-level relationship.
